extracted.intended_audience: NIH R21 applicants and biomedical researchers (NIAID applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and community discussion about what review panels and NIAID summary statements treat as strengths or weaknesses in R21 grant applications, including policy on preliminary data, investigator track record, experimental feasibility, and scoring implications. Useful to applicants preparing or revising NIH R21 proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accomplished investigator and research team
rubrics_metrics.description: “Strengths of the application include the accomplished investigator and research team.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being an accomplished investigator and having a strong research team is explicitly listed as a strength in summary statements; institutional reputation and past productivity can influence reviewers' impressions (commenters note that being at a 'rockstar' institution probably helps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong preliminary data
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple summary statements praise “strong preliminary data”, “compelling preliminary data”, or “strong and compelling preliminary data”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although R21 policy says preliminary data are not generally required, presence of strong preliminary data is repeatedly framed as a significant asset that increases reviewers' confidence and perceived likelihood of success. Commenters report that adding preliminary data on resubmission can dramatically improve scores. Anti-pattern: relying on the policy alone to omit all data may be risky in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct, doable and logical set of experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: “the direct doable and logical set of experiments” is listed among application strengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers value experiments that are clearly feasible and logically follow from the aims and hypotheses. Applications should make the experimental plan explicit, realistic, and well-justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of paradigm-shifting insights / high impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary statements cite “the likelihood of paradigm shifting insights” as a strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-impact potential and the possibility of paradigm-shifting results are treated favorably. Applicants should articulate the broader significance and transformative potential of the work where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovative use of a novel strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary: “innovative use of the novel GPS strategy” as a strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel approaches or creative application of new techniques/strategies are positively noted by reviewers. Emphasize the novelty and why the chosen strategy is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator with a strong field-specific track record
rubrics_metrics.description: “an investigator with a strong bacterial pathogenesis research track record” is cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A documented track record in the specific research area strengthens confidence in the PI’s ability to carry out the proposed studies. Cite relevant prior publications and successes to demonstrate competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellent and appropriate set of collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: “an excellent and appropriate set of collaborators” appears in the summary statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-chosen collaborators who fill methodological or expertise gaps can improve an application's score. Describe collaborator roles and why their involvement is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: High degree of confidence that important results will emerge
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary praise: “a high degree of confidence that import results will emerge from these studies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers favor projects where the team convinces them that the proposed work will yield important, interpretable results. Use preliminary data, rigorous design, and clear endpoints to increase confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: R21 policy on preliminary data: not generally required
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters quote NIH rules: “No preliminary data is [sic] generally required” and “No preliminary data are required but may be included if available.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official R21 guidance states prelim data are not required; however, practice at some ICs and study sections shows that inclusion of compelling preliminary data can still materially help. Applicants should balance policy with the norms of their specific institute/study section and consider including limited supportive data if it strengthens feasibility or impact claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of writing and explicit statement of expected outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: “I’ve found that more than half the battle is in the writing itself, and making clear what the expected outcome of the project will be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, well-structured writing that explicitly states hypotheses, expected outcomes, and how results will be interpreted helps reviewers understand the proposal and reduces the chance of vague critiques. Make aims, milestones, and success criteria easy to find.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer boilerplate: 'insufficient data' may reflect misunderstanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters note seeing “insufficient data” used repeatedly as a reviewer critique; one describes it as “meaningless dribble” when reviewers don't understand the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that some reviewer comments are generic or indicate lack of understanding. Address specific reviewer concerns on resubmission and improve clarity and justification in the application rather than assuming the critique is purely about data quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample selection bias in posted funded applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Blog author: posting only perfect-score/funded examples (rockstar apps) is “less than helpful” and commenters ask for ‘real’ apps with imperfections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using only exemplars with ideal characteristics may give applicants unrealistic models. Seek a range of examples, including more typical/resubmitted applications, to learn how reviewers actually critique common weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring mechanics and payline awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Note: “First thing you notice is that it takes a perfect score to get funded. … the study section score range starts at 1, which is then multiplied by 10 after the voting of the entire panel is averaged.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand NIH scoring (1–9 averaged, then multiplied by 10) and consult institute-specific paylines for funding likelihood. Samples of funded grants alone do not substitute for understanding the payline and institute priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural: R21s may be reviewed in separate small-grant study sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: “At least at NIAID, R21’s are reviewed in their own study sections with R03’s and R15’s (other small grants).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know where your mechanism is reviewed (e.g., combined small-grant panels) as reviewer expectations and norms (e.g., attitudes toward preliminary data) may differ by study section. Tailor applications to panel norms when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using prior high-impact publications as supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters report successes where prior high-impact published work was used as supporting preliminary evidence and influenced reviewer enthusiasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When available, cite and summarize how prior publications support feasibility or the conceptual basis of the proposal; published results can function as de facto preliminary evidence that increases reviewer confidence.
